opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to knowing what I'm good at and what I enjoy doing. When we started OctoML, a lot of the energy came from the research we'd been doing on TVM and machine learning compilation. My passion has always been the technical side: building systems, thinking about how to make machine learning run efficiently everywhere, and working with students and the open-source community.

Being a CEO is a very different job. It's about fundraising, hiring, managing a growing organization, talking with customers and investors, and making a lot of business decisions every day. Those are incredibly important skills, and I have a lot of respect for people who do it well, but it's not where I can contribute the most. If I had taken that role, I'd have spent most of my time on things I'm not best at, and less on the technology that got us started.

We were also lucky to have co-founders who were well suited to leading the company. So it made sense for me to focus on the technical vision and stay connected to research and the academic side. For me it was about putting each person where they can have the most impact. A startup is a team effort, and you don't need to hold the top title to shape where things go.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the CEO role would have meant spending most of his time on business responsibilities and less on the technology that started the company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was never really about wanting or not wanting the title. When we started OctoML, I was still deep in the technical side — TVM, the compiler stack, the research — and that's where I felt I could create the most value. Being CEO means spending most of your time on fundraising, hiring, customers, the business machinery. Those are important, and I respect people who do them well, but they're not where my strengths are, and they're not what I was excited about at the time.

I also think there's a tendency, especially in academia, to assume the person who started the project should run the company. I don't think that's right. Luis and I had worked together for years, and he was much better suited to lead the company day to day. My role was to make sure the technology direction was sound, to keep pushing the open source side, and to work with the engineering team. That division felt natural.

And frankly, I still wanted to stay close to research. I was finishing my PhD, then joining CMU as faculty. The open source community around TVM was something I cared about independently of any company, and I didn't want to give that up. So being CTO let me keep one foot in each world — which, for the kind of problems I like, is where I wanted to be.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen was deeply involved in TVM, the compiler stack, and research, where he felt he could create the most value, while CEO duties would pull him toward fundraising and business work.

astra-6.text: For me, it was really about where I could contribute the most. I like working on the technology—thinking through hard technical problems and building things with other engineers. Being CEO is a different job, and you have to want that job, with all the responsibilities that come with it. I wanted to help build Octo, but I didn’t feel that being CEO was the best way for me to do that.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen prefers technical work and that being CEO is a different job, but it does not identify giving up substantial technical work as a reason he did not want the role.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was really about where I could contribute the most. I enjoy building technology and working with the engineering team, thinking about the technical direction. Being CEO is a different job—you have to spend a lot of your time on the business, fundraising, and building the organization. Those things are essential, but I wanted to stay closer to the technology. You can help build a company without being its CEO.

r001.rationale: He says he wanted to stay closer to technology and explains that the CEO role would take substantial time away for business, fundraising, and organization-building.
